analysis.one_liner: Makes clothing brands legally responsible for wage and child-labor violations by their sewing contractors.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced in April 1997 with no cosponsors, it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999 without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Senator Edward Kennedy's bill would have made clothing manufacturers and retailers legally responsible, alongside their contractors, for minimum-wage, overtime, and child-labor violations in garment production. It also set new fines for submitting fraudulent payroll records that hide hours worked — $10,000 per act, $15,000 for a repeat offense. The bill was referred to the Senate Labor Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Garment workers — typically low-wage piece workers, many of them immigrants — who are owed minimum wage, overtime, or child-labor protections. Because contractors often shut down or declare bankruptcy before back wages are paid, the bill's key feature would let workers recover from the manufacturers and retailers upstream who have the money, and it would make those companies jointly liable for penalties too. Law-abiding sewing shops would also gain, since sweatshop operators could no longer undercut them by breaking the law — a concern the bill's own findings spell out.

how_it_helps.text: Makes every manufacturer that contracts out garment work — including retailers who arrange production, even through intermediaries — civilly liable to the same extent as the contractor for violations of minimum wage, overtime, child-labor, and industrial-homework rules, and subject to the same civil penalties.

Lets workers collect back wages directly from the manufacturer when their contractor violated wage or hour law, with joint and several liability — so an insolvent contractor no longer leaves workers with nothing.

Creates new civil penalties for payroll-record failures — up to $1,000 per affected employee — and $10,000 per act of submitting fraudulent payroll records that conceal hours worked or wage violations, rising to $15,000 for a second offense.

Targets a documented enforcement gap: the bill's findings cite the Comptroller General's conclusion that most sweatshop employers violate the Fair Labor Standards Act's recordkeeping rules, which has undermined the Labor Department's ability to collect wages owed to workers.

analysis.who_pays: Apparel manufacturers and retailers, who would bear liability and civil penalties for their contractors' wage and hour violations even when they did not directly employ the workers. Contractors who violate wage laws would face the existing penalties plus the new fines for recordkeeping failures and fraudulent payroll records. Some of the compliance cost would likely find its way into apparel prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Apparel brands, retailers, and violating contractors

drawbacks.text: Joint liability reaches companies that never directly employ the sewers: retailers and brand owners who arrange production, even indirectly through intermediaries, could be sued and penalized for a contractor's violations they may not have seen.

The added liability and penalty exposure gives brands an incentive to drop small domestic sewing shops or move production to countries where U.S. wage law does not apply — which could shrink the very domestic jobs the bill is meant to protect, since its coverage stops at the border.

The bill's own findings concede that most sweatshop employers already ignore recordkeeping rules, which suggests the deeper problem is enforcement capacity; new penalties on paper do not guarantee that the Labor Department can actually detect and pursue violations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers the bill targets, the joint-liability tool is the strongest feature, because it reaches the brands and retailers with the money to actually pay back wages — something existing law, which stops at the contractor, frequently fails to do. The real costs fall on the apparel industry: broader liability, new fines, and the risk that some brands respond by cutting off small domestic shops or moving work abroad. On balance the worker protections outweigh the compliance burden, though the bill alone would not have addressed garment work produced overseas, and it would only be as effective as the Labor Department's willingness and capacity to enforce it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Labor Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy introduced the Stop Sweatshops Act of 1997 on April 22, 1997 and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources the same day; the action record shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action ever followed.
No other senator ever cosponsored the bill, leaving Kennedy as its only Senate supporter on the record.
The bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, with the legislation still sitting in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Apparel manufacturers and retailers are better off, because they never became liable for their contractors' wage and hour violations or subject to the new penalties. Sweatshop operators who underprice law-abiding shops also kept that advantage, while the garment workers the bill was written for gained nothing.

for.name: Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it never gained a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors, and the Republican-led Senate Labor Committee never acted on it, so no vote ever revealed where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill would have made them jointly liable with their contractors for minimum-wage, overtime, and child-labor violations — reaching them even when they contracted through intermediaries. Their interest in avoiding that liability ran directly against workers trying to collect back pay.
The bill defines a retailer who contracts for garment production as a manufacturer, so store chains selling clothes could have been sued for sweatshop conditions upstream of their shelves.

Shops that violated wage and hour law would face the existing penalties plus new fines — up to $1,000 per employee for recordkeeping failures and $10,000 per fraudulent payroll record. Shops that broke the law profited at workers' expense, so their interest ran against the public.

The bill's findings state that sweatshop conditions give violators an unfair means of competition against employers who follow the law; ending that advantage would level the field for compliant shops.
